## Build and install

vc-x1 is not a build system. The config says what the steps are, the build and install commands
and where the binaries land, and vc-x1 runs them in order and checks their results: it builds
before it runs or installs, reports what it is about to copy, refuses only a copy that would be
wrong, and never lets the dev build replace the release. Cargo, not vc-x1, decides what to
rebuild.

A plain Rust crate: `cargo build` and `cargo test` of one binary, `vc-x1`, named by the
manifest's `[package].name`, which never changes. The `[build]` table in `.vc-config.md` holds two
builds, each a plain `cargo build` leaving its binary in `target/`, off the PATH, so nothing a
cycle builds replaces the `vc-x1` on the PATH until the cycle lands. Both are `--locked`, so they
compile the same dependencies, the ones `Cargo.lock` commits:

- Dev: `vc-x1 build --dev` runs `[build] dev`, `cargo build --locked`, leaving the rung's debug
  binary at `target/debug/vc-x1`. After a validation it reuses the test build, so it costs under a
  second, and `vc-x1 run --dev` runs it first, so what runs is always the current code.
- Release: `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, `cargo build --release --locked`, leaving the
  release build at `target/release/vc-x1`, its `-V` naming the commit it was built from
  ([build](#build)).
- Install: at a cycle's Land, `vc-x1 install` runs the release build, which cargo skips when
  nothing changed, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] release-dir`, after
  reporting what it is copying ([install](#install)).
- Install --dev: mid-cycle, `vc-x1 install --dev` runs the dev build, then copies it into
  `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] dev-dir`, as `vc-x1-dev`, beside the landed `vc-x1`, so the
  cycle's code can be tried from any directory ([install --dev](#install---dev)). With the
  release install, the two ways the PATH is touched.

Where each build leaves its binary is the config's to say, `[build] release-bin` and `dev-bin`:
vc-x1 never works it out from cargo or the package's name.

The commands in the order a cycle uses them, a rung's loop first and Land after:

| Command | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| `vc-x1 validate` | fmt, clippy, every test | every rung, before review |
| `vc-x1 validate --fast` | the unit tests only | while iterating |
| `vc-x1 build --dev` | the dev build, into `target/debug` | to build without running |
| `vc-x1 run --dev` | `build --dev`, then runs it | trying the change |
| `vc-x1 install --dev` | `build --dev`, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1-dev` | trying the change elsewhere |
| `vc-x1 build` | the release, into `target/release` | at Land, or to try the release profile |
| `vc-x1 run` | `build`, then runs it | the smoke check before install |
| `vc-x1 install` | `build`, then reports it and copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` | at Land |

`validate` checks the source and makes no build of either kind. `run`, `run --dev`, `install`, and
`install --dev` build first, as `cargo run` does, and cargo rebuilds only what changed, so the binary
`run` smoke-tests is the one `install` copies.

- `target/debug/vc-x1 -V` names the exact rung, since the version-of-record carries the cycle's
  suffix (`0.85.6-1`), and the binary banners the name it was invoked as (`argv[0]`), so a copy
  or a symlink self-reports truthfully.
- Before 2026-10-20 a cycle renamed the package to `vc-x1-dev` instead, guarded by `build.rs`
  (the single-name convention, 0.78.3, design record in `notes/chores/chores-16.md`). The rename
  and the guard are gone: a build script cannot see an install's root, and building off the PATH
  makes the rename unnecessary.

The first install, and any install when the `vc-x1` on the PATH is too old to have `install`, is
made from the source: `cargo run --locked -- install` builds the dev binary and has it build the
release and install it, report and all.

vc-x1 links jj-lib and refuses to run when the installed `jj`'s version disagrees with it
(override per invocation with `--allow-jj-mismatch`, and see `vc-x1 version`).

## Usage

```

vc-x1 squash -s b [--title T --body B]     # Fold the working copies into the pair

vc-x1 agent-files version                  # Print the workspace's agent-files set version, bare
vc-x1 agent-files diff [--from A] [--to B]  # Name the set files that differ between two copies of the set
vc-x1 agent-files copy [--from S] [--to D]  # Make DST's set a copy of SRC's, uncommitted

bookmark to move or the commit it is at, and `push -s b --bookmark feature` is one of them. The
command line is also what is reviewed before a write runs, and a flag says what each word means.
The same names mean the same thing everywhere:

| Flag | Means |
|------|-------|
| `-s, --scope` | Which repos: `w\|work`, `a\|agent`, `b\|both`, or `p\|por` |

172	vc-x1 agent-files copy [--from S] [--to D]  # Make DST's set a copy of SRC's, uncommitted
173	vc-x1 agent-files size [--dir DIR]         # Count the set's lines, and slide the table that records them
174	vc-x1 --version                            # Print version, with the workspace's agent-files version
175	vc-x1 --help                           # Print help
176	```
177	
178	### Every argument is a flag
179	
180	Every argument is a flag, the command names aside, so a word on the command line says what it is
181	and never reads two ways by its place: in `push -s b feature`, `feature` could have been the
182	bookmark to move or the commit it is at, and `push -s b --bookmark feature` is one of them. The
183	command line is also what is reviewed before a write runs, and a flag says what each word means.
184	The same names mean the same thing everywhere:
185	
186	| Flag | Means |
187	|------|-------|
188	| `-s, --scope` | Which repos: `w\|work`, `a\|agent`, `b\|both`, or `p\|por` |
189	| `-R, --repo` | Where: a path in the workspace, or a plain repo |
190	| `-r, --revision` | A revision, as jj resolves it, `..` notation on the read commands |
191	| `-n, --commits` | How many commits a read command shows |
192	| `--bookmark` | A bookmark's name, the one to move or a new one to create |
193	| `--file`, `--dir` | A file or a directory a command reads |
194	| `-d, --dev` | The dev build, on `build`, `install`, and `run` |
195	
196	The one exception is `run`'s trailing arguments, which are the built binary's, not vc-x1's.
197	
198	A positional a command once took is kept hidden and refused, naming the flag that replaced it with
199	the value in place, so a stale doc or a habit is told its own fix:
200	
201	```
202	$ vc-x1 push -s b @-
203	error: push: the positional is retired, every argument is a flag: `-r @-`
204	```
205	
206	`build-dev`, `install-dev`, and `run-dev` are refused the same way, naming `build --dev`, `install
207	--dev`, and `run --dev`, and `init --por` and `clone --por` name `--scope por`.
208	
209	### jj version gate
210	
211	vc-x1 embeds jj-lib and writes the same repo data the installed `jj` reads, so every subcommand
212	refuses to run when the installed `jj`'s version differs from the embedded jj-lib's. The
213	`version` subcommand is the one exception: it reports the verdict instead of acting on it, and
214	withholds its `jj-data` lines on a mismatch. The rule and its rationale live in

896	### build
897	
898	Build the workspace's release with `build`, or its dev build with `build --dev`, by the work side's
899	`[build]` table (see [Workspace config tables](#workspace-config-tables)). The lists run as
900	[validate](#validate)'s do: each element one command, split on whitespace with no shell in between,
901	run in order from the work repo root, the first failure stopping the run. Neither touches the PATH,
902	which is `vc-x1 install`'s.
903	
904	- `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, which builds the release, and then checks it left
905	  `[build] release-bin`.
906	- `vc-x1 build --dev` runs `[build] dev`, the dev build, `--dev` choosing the build as it does
907	  for `run` and `install`. The old `build-dev` is refused, naming `build --dev`.
908	- Neither tracks whether its binary is out of date: cargo does, rebuilding only what changed, so
909	  a build with nothing changed is quick and leaves the binary as it was.
910	- Both commands run their lists with two variables added to the environment,
911	  `VC_X1_BUILD_COMMIT`, the full commit id of `@-`, and `VC_X1_BUILD_STATE`, `clean` or `dirty`,
912	  so an artifact that compiles them in can say what it was built from wherever it is copied.
913	  `validate` passes the same two, so the test build it leaves has the same values and
914	  `build --dev` reuses it rather than recompiling. vc-x1 compiles them in, as semver build metadata
915	  in its banner, and as a `build` line in `vc-x1 version`:
916	
917	  ```
918	  $ target/release/vc-x1 -V
919	  vc-x1 0.85.7+d70cf9ecdfd9 (agent-files v0.3.0)
920	  ```
921	
922	  `.dirty` follows the commit when `@` was not empty. A build none of the three made, a
923	  hand-typed `cargo build` or `cargo install`, takes the commit from git's `HEAD`, which in a jj
924	  colocated repo is `@-`, and follows it with `.unknown`, since whether `@` held edits is a jj
925	  question its build script cannot ask. A build with no `.git` to read, a source package's,
926	  carries no metadata.
927	- Nothing is checked first, so a release may be built from a cycle's bookmark to try the release
928	  profile.
929	
930	```
931	# Build the release, from the workspace containing the current directory
932	vc-x1 build
933	
934	# Build the dev build without running it
935	vc-x1 build --dev
936	
937	# Print the release build's list, and run nothing
938	vc-x1 build --dry-run
939	```
940	
941	| Option | Description |
942	|--------|-------------|
943	| `--dry-run` | Print the list, and run nothing |
944	| `-R, --repo <DIR>` | Workspace to build from, for both commands [default: the one containing the current directory] |
945	
946	### install
947	
948	Build the release if it is out of date, then copy it into the install directory, at a cycle's Land.
949	It first runs `[build] release` exactly as [build](#build) does. Cargo rebuilds only what changed,
950	so with nothing changed the binary already tested is the one copied, and a missing or stale one is
951	built rather than refused. It then copies `[build] release-bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here, into
952	the one directory `[install] release-dir` names, `~/.cargo/bin` here, under the same file name.
953	`$PATH` is not searched: the directory being on it is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the
954	directory expands against your home, so the committed value fits every machine. The copy is a
955	temporary file renamed into place, so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a failed
956	copy leaves it as it was.
957	
958	`[install] release`, a command list in `[build] release`'s shape, runs in place of the copy when
959	present, after the same build, report, and refusals, so a project that installs some other way, a
960	signed copy or one to another machine, says how. The elements run with no shell, each split on
961	whitespace, and then each word's placeholders are filled: `{build.release-bin}` and
962	`{install.release-dir}`, the values of the keys `install` reads, resolved for the run, `~`
963	expanded and `--dir` applied. A value with spaces stays one word, and any other `{name}` is an
964	error before anything runs. The list names every path it writes, the file name included, and a
965	script takes the values as arguments, `sh scripts/sign.sh {build.release-bin}
966	{install.release-dir}`. This workspace's list is the copy written out, so the config says what
967	`install` does:
968	
969	```toml
970	[install]
971	release = [
972	  "cp {build.release-bin} {install.release-dir}/vc-x1.new",
973	  "mv {install.release-dir}/vc-x1.new {install.release-dir}/vc-x1",
974	]
975	release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
976	```
977	
978	The rename is what makes it safe over a running binary, since a `cp` onto a running executable
979	fails. A failed `cp` leaves the `.new` file behind, which the next install overwrites, where the
980	built-in copy removes its own. The log shows each command with its placeholders filled.
981	
982	It first reports what it is copying, from the binary's own `-V`:
983	
984	- the version, noting a suffixed (pre-release) one and a manifest version that differs
985	- the commit, and whether it is `main` and `main@origin`
986	- the state, `clean`, `dirty`, or `unknown`
987	
988	A binary whose `-V` carries no commit, another project's that does not compile the build
989	variables in, is reported as `commit unknown` and `state unknown`.
990	
991	The report refuses nothing. Which builds may be installed is the release process's call, not the
992	tool's: here a cycle's Land runs `install` on `main` after the push, and a project releasing from
993	a branch or a tag makes it differently. `install` refuses only when the copy itself would be
994	wrong, listing every reason: no binary at `release-bin` after the build, a binary whose `-V` will
995	not run, or a missing install directory.
996	
997	`--dry-run` builds and reports, and copies nothing, and runs no list. `--dir <DIR>` copies into
998	`DIR` instead of `[install] release-dir` for the one run, so a test of `install` leaves the PATH
999	alone, a relative `DIR` taken against the current directory. A workspace with no `[install]
1000	release-dir`, and no `--dir`, has nothing to install, and `install` says so before building
1001	anything.
1002	
1003	```
1004	# At Land, on main after the push: build and smoke-test, then install, its build a no-op
1005	vc-x1 build
1006	vc-x1 run -- -V
1007	vc-x1 install
1008	
1009	# Testing install itself: the copy goes to tmp/bin, and ~/.cargo/bin is untouched
1010	mkdir -p tmp/bin
1011	cargo run --locked -- install --dir tmp/bin
1012	```
1013	
1014	The report, run on a cycle's bookmark with edits in `@`, then the list:
1015	
1016	```
1017	install: '/home/me/proj/target/release/vc-x1' -> list `install.release`
1018	install:   version 0.85.7-6, a suffixed (pre-release) version
1019	install:   commit 82e97636b7f6, not `main`
1020	install:   state dirty
1021	install: [1/2] cp /home/me/proj/target/release/vc-x1 /home/me/.cargo/bin/vc-x1.new
1022	install: [2/2] mv /home/me/.cargo/bin/vc-x1.new /home/me/.cargo/bin/vc-x1
1023	install: 2 command(s) passed (install.release)
1024	```
1025	
1026	The build's own lines, `build: [1/1] cargo build --release --locked` and the rest, come first.
1027	Without a list the first line names the destination, `-> '/home/me/.cargo/bin/vc-x1'`, and the
1028	copy ends `install: copied`. A dry run stops after the report and says so, running and copying
1029	nothing.
1030	
1031	| Option | Description |
1032	|--------|-------------|
1033	| `--dry-run` | Build and report, and copy nothing |
1034	| `--dir <DIR>` | Copy into `DIR` instead of `[install] release-dir`, for this run |
1035	| `-R, --repo <DIR>` | Workspace to install from [default: the one containing the current directory] |

1037	### install --dev
1038	
1039	Build the dev build, then copy it into the install directory with `[install] dev-suffix`, `-dev`
1040	when absent, appended to its file name. It first runs `[build] dev` exactly as
1041	[build --dev](#build) does, then copies `[build] dev-bin`, `target/debug/vc-x1` here, into the directory `[install]
1042	dev-dir` or `--dir` names, as `vc-x1-dev`. The landed `vc-x1` and the cycle's `vc-x1-dev` then sit
1043	side by side on the PATH, so the dev build can be tried from any directory, another project's
1044	included, where `vc-x1 run --dev` would run that project's dev build instead. The suffix is what lets
1045	`dev-dir` be `release-dir`'s own directory, the dev build beside the release without replacing it,
1046	and without a list `install --dev` refuses before the build when its destination would be the
1047	release's, as an empty suffix in that directory or a `--dir` onto it would make it. A list writes
1048	where it says, so it names the suffix itself, `{install.dev-suffix}`, as this workspace's does.
1049	
1050	The report, the refusals, the copy, `--dry-run`, and `--dir` are [install](#install)'s, the binary
1051	being the dev build's, and an `[install] dev` list runs in place of the copy as `[install] release`
1052	does for `install`, its placeholders `{build.dev-bin}` and `{install.dev-dir}`. With a list the
1053	`-dev` name is the list's to write, as this workspace's does: a list that left it off would write
1054	the release's name and, with `dev-dir` the release's own directory, replace the release.
1055	
1056	```
1057	# Mid-cycle: put the rung's code on the PATH as vc-x1-dev, and try it in another project
1058	vc-x1 install --dev
1059	cd ../other-project
1060	vc-x1-dev status
1061	```
1062	
1063	| Option | Description |
1064	|--------|-------------|
1065	| `--dry-run` | Build and report, and copy nothing |
1066	| `--dir <DIR>` | Copy into `DIR` instead of `[install] dev-dir`, for this run |
1067	
1068	The old `install-dev` is refused, naming `install --dev`.
1069	| `-R, --repo <DIR>` | Workspace to install from [default: the one containing the current directory] |
1070	
1071	### run
1072	
1073	Build, then run the build's binary with the given arguments, as `cargo run` builds before it runs.
1074	`vc-x1 run` runs `[build] release` exactly as [build](#build) does, then `[build] release-bin`,
1075	and `vc-x1 run --dev` runs `[build] dev`, then `[build] dev-bin`, so what runs is always the current
1076	code. Neither touches the PATH, so a build is tried before [install](#install), `--dev` or not,
1077	copies it. `--dev` comes before the arguments, which are the binary's, and the old `run-dev` is
1078	refused, naming `run --dev`.
1079	
1080	- The arguments go to the binary untouched. One that starts with `-` comes after `--`, as with
1081	  `cargo run`, since vc-x1's own flags are read first: `vc-x1 run -V` prints vc-x1's banner,
1082	  and `vc-x1 run -- -V` runs the release's `-V`.
1083	- The binary runs in the current directory, with the terminal, and its exit code is vc-x1's, so
1084	  a failing run fails the same way.
1085	- Before it runs, its `-V` is read, and a version other than the manifest's is a warning naming
1086	  the key: the build passed but left an older binary where the config says. A binary whose `-V`
1087	  prints no version, another project's, is run without the check.
1088	- `--dry-run` prints the build's list and the command, and runs nothing.
1089	- Completion is the binary's own: `vc-x1 run --dev <words><TAB>` asks the dev build, in clap's
1090	  completion mode, to complete `<words>`, so in iiac-perf `vc-x1 run --dev run <TAB>` offers its
1091	  benches. The binary is asked as it stands, never built, and one that is not there, or answers
1092	  nothing, offers nothing. A binary built with clap's dynamic completion answers; another offers
1093	  nothing.
1094	
1095	```
1096	# The smoke check before install: build the release and print its version
1097	vc-x1 run -- -V
1098	
1099	# Try the rung's code: build the dev build and run its status
1100	vc-x1 run --dev status -s b
1101	
1102	# See what would run
1103	vc-x1 run --dev --dry-run status -s b
1104	```
1105	
1106	| Option | Description |
1107	|--------|-------------|
1108	| `--dry-run` | Print the build's list and the command, and run nothing |
1109	| `-R, --repo <DIR>` | Workspace to run from [default: the one containing the current directory] |
1110	| `[ARGS]...` | Arguments for the binary, after `--` when the first starts with `-` |

1307	### Workspace config tables
1308	
1309	A work-side `.vc-config.md` holds up to eight tables:
1310	
1311	- `[repos]`: the two repos' local paths, written by `init`. The one table the agent repo's config
1312	  carries too.
1313	- `[remote]` (0.84.12): remote names rather than paths. Its one key, `agent-repo`, is the
1314	  agent-repo's name on its remote, which `clone` reads before there is an agent-repo to ask.
1315	  - Only the last URL segment is recorded. The owner and the host come from the work repo's own
1316	    remote, so the two repos are siblings in one namespace.
1317	  - An absent key means a name derived from `repos.agent`'s last component: a dot-led one is
1318	    appended to the work repo's name (`.claude` gives `<name>.claude`), any other is used whole.
1319	- `[family]` (0.80.0): the agent-file family this repo belongs to, which was prose in the project
1320	  layer before.
1321	- `[validate]` (0.80.0): the commands that validate this repo, also prose in the project layer
1322	  before.
1323	- `[build]` (0.85.7): the dev and release builds, and the binaries they leave, read by `build`,
1324	  `build --dev`, `run`, `run --dev`, `install`, and `install --dev` ([Build and
1325	  install](#build-and-install)).
1326	- `[install]` (0.85.7): in `[build]`'s order, `release` and `dev`, optional lists run in place of
1327	  the copy, and `release-dir` and `dev-dir`, where `install` copies the release build and
1328	  `install --dev` the dev build, `~` expanded.
1329	- `[agent-files.diff]` and `[agent-files.copy]` (0.83.0): the defaults for the `agent-files`
1330	  commands' `DIR` operand and `--custom` choice.
1331	
1332	All but `[repos]` are work side only: `validate-config` reports them unknown in the agent repo's
1333	config.

1337	[repos]
1338	work = "."
1339	agent = ".claude"                 # the agent repo's directory, relative to this file
1340	```

1345	```

1350	template = "../vc-x1-template/work"  # the payload directory holding the pinned agent-files
1351	messages = "../vc-x1-messages"    # the family's notification repo

### Workspace config tables

A work-side `.vc-config.md` holds up to eight tables:

- `[repos]`: the two repos' local paths, written by `init`. The one table the agent repo's config
  carries too.
- `[remote]` (0.84.12): remote names rather than paths. Its one key, `agent-repo`, is the
  agent-repo's name on its remote, which `clone` reads before there is an agent-repo to ask.
  - Only the last URL segment is recorded. The owner and the host come from the work repo's own
    remote, so the two repos are siblings in one namespace.
  - An absent key means a name derived from `repos.agent`'s last component: a dot-led one is
    appended to the work repo's name (`.claude` gives `<name>.claude`), any other is used whole.
- `[family]` (0.80.0): the agent-file family this repo belongs to, which was prose in the project
  layer before.
- `[validate]` (0.80.0): the commands that validate this repo, also prose in the project layer
  before.
- `[build]` (0.85.7): the dev and release builds, and the binaries they leave, read by `build`,
  `build --dev`, `run`, `run --dev`, `install`, and `install --dev` ([Build and
  install](#build-and-install)).
- `[install]` (0.85.7): in `[build]`'s order, `release` and `dev`, optional lists run in place of
  the copy, and `release-dir` and `dev-dir`, where `install` copies the release build and
  `install --dev` the dev build, `~` expanded.
- `[agent-files.diff]` and `[agent-files.copy]` (0.83.0): the defaults for the `agent-files`
  commands' `DIR` operand and `--custom` choice.

All but `[repos]` are work side only: `validate-config` reports them unknown in the agent repo's
config.

A plain Rust crate: `cargo build` and `cargo test` of one binary, `vc-x1`, named by the
manifest's `[package].name`, which never changes. The `[build]` table in `.vc-config.md` holds two
builds, each a plain `cargo build` leaving its binary in `target/`, off the PATH, so nothing a
cycle builds replaces the `vc-x1` on the PATH until the cycle lands. Both are `--locked`, so they
compile the same dependencies, the ones `Cargo.lock` commits:

- Dev: `vc-x1 build --dev` runs `[build] dev`, `cargo build --locked`, leaving the rung's debug
  binary at `target/debug/vc-x1`. After a validation it reuses the test build, so it costs under a
  second, and `vc-x1 run --dev` runs it first, so what runs is always the current code.
- Release: `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, `cargo build --release --locked`, leaving the
  release build at `target/release/vc-x1`, its `-V` naming the commit it was built from
  ([build](#build)).
- Install: at a cycle's Land, `vc-x1 install` runs the release build, which cargo skips when
  nothing changed, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] release-dir`, after
  reporting what it is copying ([install](#install)).
- Install --dev: mid-cycle, `vc-x1 install --dev` runs the dev build, then copies it into
  `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] dev-dir`, as `vc-x1-dev`, beside the landed `vc-x1`, so the
  cycle's code can be tried from any directory ([install --dev](#install---dev)). With the
  release install, the two ways the PATH is touched.

Where each build leaves its binary is the config's to say, `[build] release-bin` and `dev-bin`:
vc-x1 never works it out from cargo or the package's name.

manifest's `[package].name`, which never changes. A build is chosen by a named profile, a
`[profile.<name>]` table in `.vc-config.md`, and `--profile NAME` on `build`, `run`, and `install`
picks one, else `[build] default-profile`, else `release`. The `[build] commands` list is one
build for every profile, a plain `cargo build --profile {profile.cargo} --locked` leaving its
binary in `target/`, off the PATH, so nothing a cycle builds replaces the `vc-x1` on the PATH until
the cycle lands. It is `--locked`, so every profile compiles the same dependencies, the ones
`Cargo.lock` commits. This workspace defines two profiles:

- Dev: `vc-x1 build --profile dev` runs `cargo build --profile dev --locked`, leaving the rung's
  debug binary at `target/debug/vc-x1`. After a validation it reuses the test build, so it costs
  under a second, and `vc-x1 run --profile dev` runs it first, so what runs is always the current
  code.
- Release: `vc-x1 build`, the default profile, runs `cargo build --profile release --locked`,
  leaving the release build at `target/release/vc-x1`, its `-V` naming the commit it was built
  from ([build](#build)).
- Install: at a cycle's Land, `vc-x1 install` runs the release build, which cargo skips when
  nothing changed, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] dir`, after reporting what
  it is copying ([install](#install)).
- Install --profile dev: mid-cycle, `vc-x1 install --profile dev` runs the dev build, then copies
  it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1-dev`, the profile's `suffix` appended, beside the landed
  `vc-x1`, so the cycle's code can be tried from any directory ([install
  --profile](#install---profile)). Any other profile, a soak's release candidate among them,
  installs the same way under its own suffix.

Where each build leaves its binary is the config's to say, each profile's `bin`: vc-x1 never
works it out from cargo or the package's name.

It first runs `[build] release` exactly as [build](#build) does. Cargo rebuilds only what changed,

built rather than refused. It then copies `[build] release-bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here, into
the one directory `[install] release-dir` names, `~/.cargo/bin` here, under the same file name.
`$PATH` is not searched: the directory being on it is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the
directory expands against your home, so the committed value fits every machine. The copy is a
temporary file renamed into place, so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a failed
copy leaves it as it was.

`[install] release`, a command list in `[build] release`'s shape, runs in place of the copy when
present, after the same build, report, and refusals, so a project that installs some other way, a
signed copy or one to another machine, says how. The elements run with no shell, each split on
whitespace, and then each word's placeholders are filled: `{build.release-bin}` and
`{install.release-dir}`, the values of the keys `install` reads, resolved for the run, `~`
expanded and `--dir` applied. A value with spaces stays one word, and any other `{name}` is an
error before anything runs. The list names every path it writes, the file name included, and a
script takes the values as arguments, `sh scripts/sign.sh {build.release-bin}
{install.release-dir}`. This workspace's list is the copy written out, so the config says what
`install` does:

```toml
[install]
release = [
  "cp {build.release-bin} {install.release-dir}/vc-x1.new",
  "mv {install.release-dir}/vc-x1.new {install.release-dir}/vc-x1",
]
release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
```

### install --dev

Build the dev build, then copy it into the install directory with `[install] dev-suffix`, `-dev`
when absent, appended to its file name. It first runs `[build] dev` exactly as
[build --dev](#build) does, then copies `[build] dev-bin`, `target/debug/vc-x1` here, into the directory `[install]
dev-dir` or `--dir` names, as `vc-x1-dev`. The landed `vc-x1` and the cycle's `vc-x1-dev` then sit
side by side on the PATH, so the dev build can be tried from any directory, another project's
included, where `vc-x1 run --dev` would run that project's dev build instead. The suffix is what lets
`dev-dir` be `release-dir`'s own directory, the dev build beside the release without replacing it,
and without a list `install --dev` refuses before the build when its destination would be the
release's, as an empty suffix in that directory or a `--dir` onto it would make it. A list writes
where it says, so it names the suffix itself, `{install.dev-suffix}`, as this workspace's does.

The report, the refusals, the copy, `--dry-run`, and `--dir` are [install](#install)'s, the binary
being the dev build's, and an `[install] dev` list runs in place of the copy as `[install] release`
does for `install`, its placeholders `{build.dev-bin}` and `{install.dev-dir}`. With a list the
`-dev` name is the list's to write, as this workspace's does: a list that left it off would write
the release's name and, with `dev-dir` the release's own directory, replace the release.

```

content.content:
### install

Build the chosen profile if it is out of date, then copy it into the install directory, the release
at a cycle's Land. The profile is chosen as [build](#build)'s is, and `install` first runs
`[build] commands` exactly as `build` does. Cargo rebuilds only what changed, so with nothing
changed the binary already tested is the one copied, and a missing or stale one is built rather
than refused. It then copies the profile's `bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here for the release, into
the one directory `[install] dir` names, `~/.cargo/bin` here, under the same file name with the
profile's `suffix` appended, empty when absent. `$PATH` is not searched: the directory being on it
is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the directory expands against your home, so the committed
value fits every machine. The copy is a temporary file renamed into place, so a running copy of the
old binary is undisturbed and a failed copy leaves it as it was.

`[install] commands`, a command list in `[build] commands`' shape, runs in place of the copy for
every profile when present, after the same build, report, and refusals, so a project that installs
some other way, a signed copy or one to another machine, says how. The elements run with no shell,
each split on whitespace, and then each word's placeholders are filled: `{profile.<property>}` from
the chosen profile, `{profile.bin}` and `{profile.suffix}` among them, and `{install.dir}`,
resolved for the run, `~` expanded and `--dir` applied. A value with spaces stays one word, and
any other `{name}` is an error before anything runs. The list names every path it writes, the file
name and suffix included, and a script takes the values as arguments,
`sh scripts/sign.sh {profile.bin} {install.dir}`. This workspace's list is the copy written out,
so the config says what `install` does:

```toml
[install]
dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
commands = [
  "cp {profile.bin} {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}.new",
  "mv {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}.new {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}",
]
```

The rename is what makes it safe over a running binary, since a `cp` onto a running executable
fails. A failed `cp` leaves the `.new` file behind, which the next install overwrites, where the
built-in copy removes its own. The log shows each command with its placeholders filled.

It first reports what it is copying, from the binary's own `-V`:

- the version, noting a suffixed (pre-release) one and a manifest version that differs
- the commit, and whether it is `main` and `main@origin`
- the state, `clean`, `dirty`, or `unknown`

A binary whose `-V` carries no commit, another project's that does not compile the build
variables in, is reported as `commit unknown` and `state unknown`.

The report refuses nothing. Which builds may be installed is the release process's call, not the
tool's: here a cycle's Land runs `install` on `main` after the push, and a project releasing from
a branch or a tag makes it differently. `install` refuses only when the copy itself would be
wrong, listing every reason: no binary at the profile's `bin` after the build, a binary whose `-V`
will not run, or a missing install directory. Without a list, a copy whose installed name is
another profile's in the same directory, the same file name and suffix, is refused before the
build, so a second profile with no suffix never replaces the release. A list writes where it says,
so it names the suffix itself, as this workspace's does.

`--dry-run` builds and reports, and copies nothing, and runs no list. `--dir <DIR>` copies into
`DIR` instead of `[install] dir` for the one run, so a test of `install` leaves the PATH alone, a
relative `DIR` taken against the current directory. A workspace with no `[install] dir`, and no
`--dir`, has nothing to install, and `install` says so before building anything.

```
# At Land, on main after the push: build and smoke-test, then install, its build a no-op
vc-x1 build
vc-x1 run -- -V
vc-x1 install

# Testing install itself: the copy goes to tmp/bin, and ~/.cargo/bin is untouched
mkdir -p tmp/bin
cargo run --locked -- install --dir tmp/bin
```

The report, run on a cycle's bookmark with edits in `@`, then the list:

```
install: '/home/me/proj/target/release/vc-x1' -> list `install.commands`
install:   version 0.85.7-6, a suffixed (pre-release) version
install:   commit 82e97636b7f6, not `main`
install:   state dirty
install: [1/2] cp /home/me/proj/target/release/vc-x1 /home/me/.cargo/bin/vc-x1.new

changed the binary already tested is the one copied, and a missing or stale one is built rather
than refused. It then copies the profile's `bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here for the release, into
the one directory `[install] dir` names, `~/.cargo/bin` here, under the same file name with the
profile's `suffix` appended, empty when absent. `$PATH` is not searched: the directory being on it
is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the directory expands against your home, so the committed
value fits every machine. The copy is a temporary file renamed into place, so a running copy of the
old binary is undisturbed and a failed copy leaves it as it was.

`[install] commands`, a command list in `[build] commands`' shape, runs in place of the copy for
every profile when present, after the same build, report, and refusals, so a project that installs
some other way, a signed copy or one to another machine, says how. The elements run with no shell,
each split on whitespace, and then each word's placeholders are filled: `{profile.<property>}` from
the chosen profile, `{profile.bin}` and `{profile.suffix}` among them, and `{install.dir}`,
